6.about: Scriabin’s first sonata is the confession of a personal crisis. In 1891, pushing himself to master repertoire built around wide stretches and octave technique, he damaged his right hand badly enough to threaten his career as a pianist, and the disorientation of that year colours the whole work. The opening Allegro con fuoco is urgent and unsettled, closer in spirit to Chopin than to anything Scriabin would later write. A melancholy Adagio in C minor follows, an inward, songful movement. The Presto that comes next never quite resolves its own agitation, and instead of a conventional finale it drives straight into a Funebre: a slow, tolling funeral march that closes the sonata not in triumph but in mourning, following the model Chopin had set in his own B-flat minor Sonata half a century earlier. For a composer’s first published sonata, it is a strikingly dark and personal statement.
6.ctx: The hand injury of 1891 came after months of obsessive practising, and Scriabin appears never to have discussed it publicly in any detail, but pianists and biographers have long read the sonata’s funeral-march ending as his response to a year in which he feared his career as a musician was over. He recovered enough use of the hand to keep performing and composing for another two decades, and later works composed for the left hand alone are sometimes connected to the same period of enforced one-handed practice. The sonata was published in 1893, and its debts to Chopin — in its figuration, its funeral march, and its general Romantic temperament — are audible throughout; the more exotic, mystical Scriabin of the later sonatas is not yet in evidence.
parts: An urgent, unsettled opening movement, close in spirit to Chopin.
Restless and unresolved, leading straight into the finale.
A slow, tolling funeral march that closes the sonata in mourning rather than triumph.
facts: Written in 1892, after a hand injury in 1891 that Scriabin feared would end his career as a pianist.
Its funeral-march finale follows the model of Chopin’s Sonata No. 2 in B-flat minor.
Henle rates it level 8.

19.about: Scriabin’s Second Sonata is a seascape in two movements, one of the first works in which he replaced the classical four-movement plan with a compact, contrasting pair. He began sketching it as early as 1892 but kept revising it for years, performing it in Paris in 1896 while still dissatisfied with the result, and only pronounced himself happy with it in 1898 after what he described as seven rounds of revision. The first movement, Andante, is calm and undulating, and Scriabin associated it with the stillness of a southern sea by moonlight; the second, a stormy Presto, sweeps that calm away in restless, agitated figuration, as though the same sea had risen into a squall. The contrast between repose and turbulence would recur throughout his later sonatas, though here it is still handled with a Romantic, almost pictorial directness he would soon abandon.
19.ctx: The subtitle ‘Sonata-Fantasy’ signals Scriabin’s own sense that the two-movement, contrast-driven design departed from what a sonata conventionally meant in the 1890s. He composed and revised it during the years he was establishing himself as a touring virtuoso across Russia and western Europe, and its long gestation — sketches reaching back to 1892, the finished score not settled until 1898 — is unusual among his sonatas, most of which he wrote quickly. Because the printed first edition left some passages ambiguous, Scriabin’s own performance of the work, preserved on paper rolls for a maker of mechanical pianos, has since been used by editors to help settle questions the score alone does not answer.
parts: A calm, undulating movement Scriabin linked to a still, moonlit sea.
A stormy, turbulent movement that sweeps the opening’s calm away.
facts: Scriabin linked the two movements to a calm sea and then a storm.
He revised the sonata for roughly six years before he was satisfied with it.
Henle rates it level 8.

20.about: Scriabin’s only concerto and one of the very few large-scale works he wrote for piano and orchestra, cast in a warm, lyrical style closer to Chopin’s two piano concertos than to the harmonically radical music Scriabin would write only a decade later. The outer movements are brilliant but never overwhelming, while the central Andante is a gentle theme and variations that lets the soloist sing above a light orchestral accompaniment.
20.ctx: Composed in 1896–97, while Scriabin was still establishing himself as a touring virtuoso pianist, the concerto was premiered in Odessa in October 1897 with the composer himself at the keyboard. It was dedicated to Vasily Safonov, the director of the Moscow Conservatory who had taught Scriabin piano, and it remains the only concerto in his output — he never returned to the genre, focusing his later large-scale ambitions on the purely orchestral tone poems Poem of Ecstasy and Prometheus instead.
parts: A brilliant but lyrical opening movement, closer to Chopin than to Scriabin’s later style.
A gentle theme and variations for soloist and orchestra.
facts: Scriabin’s only piano concerto and one of his few large works for piano and orchestra.
Premiered in Odessa in 1897 with Scriabin himself as soloist.
Dedicated to Vasily Safonov, his piano teacher at the Moscow Conservatory.

23.about: The Third Sonata is the last of Scriabin’s sonatas built on the classical four-movement plan, and one of the finest achievements of his early, Chopin- and Liszt-influenced style. Scriabin later attached a loose programme to it, describing its four movements as states of the soul: a turbulent, unfree struggle; a moment of fleeting, illusory happiness; a mournful, contemplative calm; and finally a struggle that breaks free into an elemental, triumphant finale. Musically the sonata is tightly integrated for a four-movement work of its period, with material recurring and transforming across the span, and it demands both the sweep and the stamina of a Lisztian virtuoso.
23.ctx: Composed in the mid-to-late 1890s, the sonata belongs to the final stretch of Scriabin’s career before his harmonic language began to drift toward the exotic and, eventually, the atonal soundworld of his last sonatas. It remains one of his most frequently performed and recorded works, prized by pianists for the way it combines that late-Romantic virtuosity with real structural coherence, and it often serves as a bridge for listeners between the Chopin-indebted First Sonata and the single-movement, mystically charged works that follow from the Fifth Sonata onward.
parts: A turbulent opening movement of unresolved struggle.
A brief, fleeting movement of illusory happiness.
A finale in which struggle breaks free into a triumphant close.
facts: Scriabin later described its four movements as depicting states of the soul, from struggle to triumph.
It is the last of his sonatas built on the classical four-movement plan.
Henle rates it level 8.

26.about: Scriabin’s First Symphony is an unusually ambitious six-movement work that ends, unconventionally for a symphony, with a choral finale for soprano and tenor soloists and chorus setting Scriabin’s own text in praise of art as a unifying, quasi-religious force — an early sign of the mystical ambitions that would grow across his career.
26.ctx: Composed in 1899–1900, the symphony was Scriabin’s most substantial orchestral undertaking to date and his first major statement outside the piano music on which his early reputation rested. Its hymn-like choral finale anticipates the philosophical and mystical preoccupations of his later orchestral works, including the Poem of Ecstasy.
26.sc: Soprano and tenor soloists, chorus, orchestra
facts: Ends with a choral finale praising art, sung to Scriabin’s own text.
Scriabin’s first large-scale orchestral work.
Anticipates the mystical ambitions of his later orchestral music.

28.about: A substantial, virtuosic single-movement fantasy from the turn of the century, standing between the four-movement sonatas of Scriabin’s early period and the free single-movement forms he would favour from the Fourth Sonata onward. Sweeping and rhetorical, it demands both the stamina and the sweep of a full-scale Romantic showpiece.
28.ctx: Composed in 1900, shortly before the First Symphony, the Fantasy shows Scriabin working at large scale within a single continuous span, a formal experiment that anticipates the one-movement sonatas and poems that would dominate the rest of his output.
facts: A large-scale, single-movement work anticipating Scriabin’s later one-movement sonatas.
Composed in 1900, shortly before his First Symphony.

29.about: A darker, more turbulent work than the First Symphony, in five continuous movements, moving from a stormy opening to a triumphant C major close. Its harmonic reach and orchestral ambition mark a clear step toward the more individual voice of Scriabin’s Third Symphony, the ‘Divine Poem’.
29.ctx: Composed in 1901, the symphony received a mixed early reception — the conductor and fellow composer Rimsky-Korsakov reportedly found parts of it bewildering — but it has since come to be seen as an important transitional work bridging Scriabin’s earlier, Romantic idiom and the visionary orchestral works of his maturity.
facts: Cast in five continuous movements rather than the usual four.
Received a mixed reception at its premiere, reportedly puzzling even Rimsky-Korsakov.
Moves from a stormy C minor opening to a triumphant C major close.

30.about: The Fourth Sonata is the hinge on which Scriabin’s sonata output turns: still cast in two linked movements rather than one, but already saturated with the yearning, ecstatic harmonic language of his mature style. Scriabin described the piece in terms of flight toward a distant star — a dreamy, luminous Andante that gradually gathers momentum, leading without a break into a Prestissimo volando (‘flying’) finale whose glittering figuration and soaring trills evoke exactly that image of ecstatic ascent. The same imagery, and much of the same harmonic world, would soon return on a far larger scale in his orchestral Poem of Ecstasy.
30.ctx: Composed in 1903, not long before Scriabin’s style tipped decisively toward the single-movement, mystically titled works of his last years, the Fourth Sonata is often treated as the true beginning of ‘late Scriabin’ even though two more numbered sonatas would still use more than one movement. Its trajectory from a hushed, searching opening to a blazing, virtuosic close became a template he returned to again and again, and pianists and scholars alike often point to it as the moment his music stopped merely resembling Chopin and Liszt and started sounding unmistakably like itself.
parts: A dreamy, luminous opening that gradually gathers momentum.
A glittering, virtuosic finale of ecstatic, soaring flight.
facts: Scriabin associated the sonata with the image of flight toward a distant star.
Its harmonic world anticipates the orchestral Poem of Ecstasy, written soon after.
Henle rates it level 8.

34.about: A single-movement work whose title announces its mood: a dark, weighty piece built from a stern opening idea that returns transformed and unresolved. Part of a run of standalone ‘poems’ Scriabin wrote in the prolific year 1903.
34.ctx: Composed in 1903, in the same extraordinarily productive year as the Fourth Sonata and the Two Poems, Op. 32, as Scriabin increasingly favoured single-movement forms with evocative titles over traditional genres.
facts: One of several free-standing ‘poems’ Scriabin composed in his highly productive year of 1903.
Its title reflects the dark, unresolved character of the music.

36.about: A restless, agitated poem whose title points to the darker, more theatrical strain running through Scriabin’s imagination even in his middle years, well before the explicitly demonic character of his very late works such as the Ninth Sonata.
36.ctx: Composed in 1903, the piece anticipates, in its title if not yet fully in its harmonic language, the fascination with dark and transgressive imagery that would become more pronounced in Scriabin’s late work.
facts: Its title anticipates the darker, quasi-demonic imagery of Scriabin’s later works.
Composed in the same fertile year, 1903, as the Fourth Sonata.

38.about: A graceful, expansive waltz, more substantial than a typical salon dance, that shows Scriabin’s early fondness for Chopin-derived forms stretched toward the harmonic richness of his middle period.
38.ctx: Composed in 1903, in the same year as the Fourth Sonata and several of Scriabin’s free-standing poems, the waltz looks back to the drawing-room genres of his early training even as his harmonic language was rapidly evolving.
facts: One of Scriabin’s few large-scale waltzes for piano.
Composed in his highly productive year of 1903.

43.about: Scriabin’s Third Symphony, subtitled ‘The Divine Poem,’ is his last symphony in a traditional multi-movement format and the work that marks his decisive turn toward the large-scale, philosophically programmatic orchestral music of his later career. Scriabin attached a detailed programme to it, describing the evolution of the human spirit through struggle and sensual pleasure toward a final, divine, playful freedom, and the three movements are titled accordingly: Luttes (Struggles), Voluptés (Delights) and Jeu divin (Divine Play).
43.ctx: Composed between 1902 and 1904 and premiered in Paris in 1905 under Arthur Nikisch, the symphony was Scriabin’s most ambitious orchestral statement to date and a clear step toward the single-movement tone poems, Poem of Ecstasy and Prometheus, that would follow it. Its philosophical programme, drawn from Scriabin’s own increasingly mystical worldview, reflects the influence of contemporary theosophical and Nietzschean ideas that shaped his thinking throughout his later career.
parts: ‘Delights’ — a sensuous, warmly orchestrated slow movement.
facts: Scriabin’s last symphony in a traditional multi-movement format.
Its three movements are titled Struggles, Delights and Divine Play, after Scriabin’s own programme.
Premiered in Paris in 1905 under Arthur Nikisch.

53.about: The Fifth Sonata was the first Scriabin cast in a single continuous movement, a form he never abandoned again. He wrote it in a burst of about six days in December 1907, though its ideas had been forming for longer, and called it, without much modesty, the best thing he had written for the piano. It shares its literary programme with the vast orchestral Poem of Ecstasy, composed around the same time, and its music traces something like the same arc: a hushed, mysterious opening; waves of yearning and struggle; and passages of glittering, ecstatic virtuosity that push the pianist to the outer edge of what the instrument can do. Scriabin prefaced the printed score with lines from his own Poem of Ecstasy, making the connection between the two works explicit.
53.ctx: Scriabin completed the sonata in Lausanne while he and his family were living abroad, just after finishing the orchestral Poem of Ecstasy, of which he considered it something of a piano companion piece. In a letter written as he was finishing it, he described the sonata as pouring out of him like a fountain, unlike anything he had written before. It was quickly recognised as one of the most difficult and demanding works in his entire output, and remains a favourite closing piece for pianists specialising in his music.
parts: Free tonality, centred loosely on F-sharp
A single continuous movement moving from a hushed, mysterious opening through struggle to ecstatic virtuosity.
facts: The first of Scriabin’s sonatas cast in a single continuous movement, a form he kept for the rest of his life.
Composed in a burst of about six days in December 1907.
Henle rates it level 9.

54.about: A vast single-movement tone poem for large orchestra and Scriabin’s first major purely orchestral statement of the mystical, ecstatic philosophy that would dominate the rest of his career. Scriabin prefaced the score with his own lengthy poem describing the human spirit’s flight from struggle through play and desire to a final, overwhelming ecstasy, and the music follows a similar arc, building continuously across some twenty minutes toward a blazing, brass-heavy climax.
54.ctx: Composed between 1905 and 1907 while Scriabin was living outside Russia, the Poem of Ecstasy was premiered in Paris in December 1908 and remains, alongside Prometheus, one of his two most frequently performed orchestral works. Its harmonic language, built increasingly around Scriabin’s own ‘mystic chord,’ pushes conventional tonality to its limits without abandoning it entirely, and it shares its underlying programme with the Fifth Piano Sonata, composed around the same time and prefaced with lines from the same poem.
54.sc: 3 flutes, piccolo, 3 oboes, English horn, 3 clarinets, 3 bassoons, 8 horns, 5 trumpets, 3 trombones, tuba, timpani, percussion, 2 harps, organ, strings
facts: Prefaced in the score by Scriabin’s own poem describing the spirit’s flight to ecstasy.
Shares its programme with the Fifth Piano Sonata, composed around the same time.
Premiered in Paris in December 1908.

60.about: Scriabin’s most ambitious and unusual orchestral work, scored for a huge orchestra, wordless chorus, prominent solo piano part, and a ‘clavier à lumières’ — a keyboard instrument of Scriabin’s own devising intended to project coloured light onto a screen in time with the music, an early and genuinely visionary attempt at synesthetic, multi-sensory performance. The music itself is built almost entirely from Scriabin’s ‘mystic chord,’ a six-note harmony stacked in fourths that replaces conventional major and minor triads throughout the piece.
60.ctx: Composed between 1908 and 1910 and premiered in Moscow in March 1911, Prometheus reflects Scriabin’s deepening interest in theosophy and his own idiosyncratic mystical philosophy in the last years of his life. The light-projection part was rarely realised in performance during Scriabin’s lifetime — the technology of the day struggled to keep up with his ambitions — and it remains a technical challenge for orchestras attempting a full staged performance even now, though the work is regularly performed as a purely orchestral piece without the lighting element.
60.sc: Large orchestra, solo piano, wordless chorus, clavier à lumières (colour organ)
facts: Calls for a ‘clavier à lumières,’ a light-projecting keyboard instrument Scriabin invented for the piece.
Built almost entirely from Scriabin’s ‘mystic chord.’
Premiered in Moscow in March 1911.

61.about: A dreamlike, harmonically suspended single-movement work combining the free lyricism of Scriabin’s ‘poems’ with the hushed, static quality of a nocturne, written in the dense chordal language of his final years.
61.ctx: Composed in 1911, in the period following the massive orchestral Prometheus, when Scriabin’s piano writing increasingly explored harmonic stasis and shimmering, bell-like sonorities in place of conventional melody and accompaniment.
facts: Combines the free form of Scriabin’s ‘poems’ with the hushed character of a nocturne.
Composed in the period following his large orchestral work Prometheus: The Poem of Fire.

62.about: The Sixth Sonata is the strangest and, by Scriabin’s own account, the most frightening of his ten. Cast in a single movement marked ‘mysterious, concentrated,’ it unfolds in a harmonic language poised on the edge of atonality, built from the same synthetic ‘mystic chord’ sonorities that underpin Prometheus. Passages of dreamlike stillness are repeatedly interrupted by eruptions the composer marked in the score as moments where terror surges up, and the music never fully resolves the tension between the two. Scriabin reportedly never played the piece in a public concert, saying its darkness disturbed him too much, even though he had composed and premiered virtually everything else he wrote himself.
62.ctx: Composed in 1911, the sonata was actually finished before the Seventh even though it carries the lower number — Scriabin composed and published the two slightly out of order. Its first public performance was given not by the composer but by the pianist Elena Bekman-Shcherbina, in Moscow the following year. The sonata’s harmonic world, built around the six-note ‘mystic chord’ Scriabin developed for Prometheus, pushes conventional tonality to its limit without quite abandoning it, and it is often singled out by pianists and scholars as the most unsettling and least assimilable of the whole cycle.
parts: Free tonality, loosely centred on G
A single, continuous movement alternating dreamlike stillness with sudden eruptions of terror.
facts: Scriabin reportedly never performed it in public, saying its darkness disturbed him.
Its first performance was given by the pianist Elena Bekman-Shcherbina in Moscow in 1912.
Henle rates it level 9.

64.about: Scriabin’s Seventh Sonata carries the nickname ‘White Mass,’ picking up on the ‘Black Mass’ title later attached to the Ninth; unlike that one, this nickname may have come from the composer himself. It is single-movement, luminous and bell-like in its sonorities, built from chiming, resonant chords that Scriabin surrounded with ecstatic, almost liturgical performance directions in the score — markings rare even by his own standards. Scriabin considered it one of the purest expressions of the mystical, quasi-religious world his late piano music was reaching toward.
64.ctx: Composed in 1911, alongside the Sixth Sonata, during the period when Scriabin was working out ideas that would feed into his unrealised, multi-sensory ‘Mysterium.’ The extraordinarily detailed, ecstatic performance directions in the autograph manuscript, since reproduced in facsimile, give an unusually direct window into how precisely Scriabin heard the piece in his own mind, down to the exact shading of touch he wanted at each climax.
parts: A single movement built from chiming, bell-like sonorities and ecstatic performance markings.
facts: Nicknamed the ‘White Mass’ sonata.
Composed in 1911, alongside the Sixth Sonata.
Henle rates it level 9.

66.about: The Eighth is Scriabin’s longest sonata and, by common consent among pianists, one of his hardest: its pages are often laid out on three or even four staves at once rather than the usual two, just to accommodate the density of its counterpoint and the sheer span of its chords. Scriabin thought of it, alongside the Sixth, as touching on the most tragic vein in his output, though its character is less openly violent than the Sixth or Seventh — its climaxes build with a kind of held-back intensity rather than exploding outright. He worked on it with unusual care, proofreading it intensively, though a number of errors still crept into the early editions.
66.ctx: Composed in 1912–13, in the same burst of activity that produced the Ninth and Tenth Sonatas, the Eighth is often the least performed of the late sonatas simply because of its length and difficulty, but specialists in Scriabin’s music regard it highly for its sustained, large-scale structure — closer in ambition to a single symphonic movement than to a conventional piano sonata. Like the Sixth Sonata, Scriabin reportedly avoided performing it in public himself.
parts: A long, densely contrapuntal single movement, Scriabin’s longest sonata by some margin.
facts: Scriabin’s longest sonata, often printed on three or four staves per system rather than two.
He proofread it with unusual care, though errors still reached the first edition.
Henle rates it level 9.

68.about: The Ninth Sonata’s nickname, ‘Black Mass,’ was not coined by Scriabin, but he approved of it and it has stuck ever since; he wrote of the piece that in it he came closer than ever before to something satanic. Its themes, built heavily around the unstable interval of a minor ninth, are transformed continuously across the sonata’s single span, from an unsettling opening trill through a grotesque march to a climax as harsh as anything else in his output, before the opening material returns to close the work. Scriabin himself gave its first performance.
68.ctx: Composed around 1912–13 alongside the Eighth and Tenth Sonatas, the Ninth is one of the most overtly demonic and dissonant works Scriabin wrote, and its ‘Black Mass’ nickname — sitting opposite the ‘White Mass’ title attached to the Seventh — reflects a real fascination on Scriabin’s part with mystical, and by his own account satanic, ideas in his final years. It remains, alongside the Sixth, one of the sonatas most often cited as evidence of how far his harmonic language had travelled from the Chopin-influenced First Sonata composed barely two decades earlier.
parts: Moderato quasi andante – Allegro molto – Presto
Free tonality, built on the minor ninth
A continuously transforming single movement, from an unsettling trill through a grotesque march to a harsh climax.
facts: Nicknamed the ‘Black Mass’ sonata; Scriabin approved the name though he did not coin it.
Scriabin himself gave its first performance.
Henle rates it level 9.

69.about: Two brief, terse late pieces, composed in the harmonically ambiguous, atonal-leaning idiom Scriabin developed in his final years, a world away from the Chopin-influenced style of his early préludes and études.
69.ctx: Composed in 1913, close to the end of Scriabin’s life, when his music had moved into free chromaticism built from his own harmonic vocabulary rather than conventional major-minor tonality.
facts: Written in 1913, within Scriabin’s final, most harmonically radical period.
One of several sets of very short late pieces he composed in his last years.

70.about: Scriabin’s last completed sonata is also his sunniest late work, full of shimmering trills and fluttering, rapid figuration that the composer connected to insects — he reportedly called it his ‘insect sonata,’ hearing in its trills the sound of kisses, or of insects born from the sun. Where the Sixth and Ninth sonatas explore darkness and terror, the Tenth is radiant and sensuous, its harmonic mysticism turned toward light rather than dread, and its trills function almost as a texture in their own right, running through nearly the entire piece.
70.ctx: Composed in the winter of 1912–13, alongside the Eighth and Ninth Sonatas, the Tenth was the last sonata Scriabin completed before his death in 1915; he continued sketching further large-scale, mystically conceived projects afterward, including the unrealised ‘Mysterium’ and its preparatory ‘Acte préalable,’ but wrote no further numbered sonatas. Pianists and scholars often single it out as the most immediately beautiful of the late sonatas, less forbidding than the Sixth or Ninth despite sharing much of the same harmonic vocabulary.
parts: A single movement built almost entirely from shimmering, insect-like trills.
facts: Scriabin reportedly called it his ‘insect sonata,’ linking its trills to insects and kisses.
The last sonata he completed before his death in 1915.
Henle rates it level 9.

71.about: Two of the very last pieces Scriabin completed, composed the year before his death, in the dense, ambiguous harmonic language of his final period — music that seems to dissolve conventional tonality almost entirely.
71.ctx: Composed in 1914, among the last works Scriabin wrote before his sudden death from blood poisoning in April 1915, at the height of his ambitions for the never-completed Mysterium.
facts: Among the last pieces Scriabin completed before his death in 1915.
Written in the extremely chromatic, tonality-dissolving idiom of his final years.

72.about: One of the most extraordinary single pages in the entire piano repertoire: a short, unbroken crescendo from a hushed, flickering opening to an overwhelming, bell-like climax, without a single bar of relief along the way. The piece is built almost entirely from trembling repeated notes and tremolandos that never stop, creating the illusion of a sound constantly growing brighter and hotter — Scriabin himself associated the piece with fire and light, consistent with the mystical, synesthetic ideas that dominated his final years.
72.ctx: Composed in 1914, the year before Scriabin’s sudden death, Vers la flamme (‘Toward the Flame’) was originally sketched as a possible eleventh piano sonata before Scriabin decided it worked better as a self-contained tone poem for piano. It shares its harmonic world and obsessive, unbroken intensity with the very late sonatas, and pianists regard it as one of the most punishing short pieces in his output, both for its stamina demands and for the difficulty of sustaining a single, continuous crescendo convincingly across several minutes.
facts: Originally sketched as a possible eleventh piano sonata before becoming a stand-alone piece.
Composed in 1914, the year before Scriabin’s death.
Henle rates it level 8.

73.about: Two contrasting late dances — the first, ‘Guirlandes’ (Garlands), light and decorative, the second, ‘Flammes sombres’ (Dark Flames), turbulent and driven — composed in the dense, ambiguous harmonic language of Scriabin’s final period.
73.ctx: Composed in 1914, among the last works Scriabin completed before his death the following year, as he continued sketching his vast, unfinished project the Mysterium, of which these late miniatures share the harmonic world.
facts: Comprises two contrasting dances, ‘Guirlandes’ (Garlands) and ‘Flammes sombres’ (Dark Flames).
Composed in 1914, one of Scriabin’s last completed sets of piano pieces.

74.about: Five terse, aphoristic préludes, Scriabin’s very last completed work, written in an extremely compressed, atonal-leaning language stripped of almost everything but its harmonic essence — a striking contrast to the lush, Chopin-derived préludes of Op. 11 written a quarter-century earlier.
74.ctx: Composed in 1914 and published shortly after Scriabin’s sudden death in April 1915, the Five Préludes are the last notes he set down, offering a glimpse of where his radical late harmonic language might have led had he lived to complete the Mysterium he had spent his final years planning.
facts: Scriabin’s last completed work, finished the year before his death.
Extremely brief and harmonically radical compared with his early préludes, Op. 11.
Published posthumously in 1915.

2/1.about: One of Scriabin’s best-known piano pieces is also one of his very first: he wrote it at only fifteen, and when it was finally printed in 1893, the twenty-one-year-old composer was still so unknown that he received no payment for it at all. Marked Andante, it is not a virtuoso showpiece — its challenge lies instead in voicing full, legato chords so that an inner melody sings out clearly above a murmuring lower texture, a very Chopin-like problem that Scriabin would return to throughout his career. Its aching, songful melody made it an immediate favourite, and it remains the single most-performed piece he ever wrote.
2/1.ctx: Composed in 1887 and published as the first of the two Op. 2 pieces in 1893, the étude predates by several years the harmonic experiments that would make Scriabin famous, and it shows instead how thoroughly he had absorbed Chopin’s nocturne style while still a teenager at the Moscow Conservatory. Its lasting popularity has made it, alongside the ‘Black Mass’ and ‘White Mass’ sonatas, one of the handful of Scriabin works that listeners who know nothing else by him are likely to recognise.
facts: Composed when Scriabin was only fifteen years old.
He received no payment when it was first published in 1893.
Henle rates it level 4, one of the easiest pieces of his to enter a recital programme.

8/12.about: Nicknamed ‘Patetico,’ this is Scriabin’s most popular virtuoso showpiece and one of the great encore pieces of the whole Romantic repertoire — a concert by Vladimir Horowitz without it, Henle’s own editors note, was almost unthinkable. Built from explosive octaves in the right hand hammered out over wide, athletic leaps in the left, it unleashes what its title promises: a short, passionate frenzy that rarely lets up from its opening bar to its final chord.
8/12.ctx: Composed in 1894–95 as the last of the Twelve Études, Op. 8, the piece belongs to Scriabin’s early period, still close in spirit to Chopin and Liszt rather than to the mystical harmonic world of his later music, but already pushing toward the physically extreme, self-punishing virtuosity that would mark much of his writing for the rest of his life. It has remained a favourite of touring virtuoso pianists ever since, prized as much for its sheer theatrical excitement as for its craftsmanship.
facts: A favourite encore of Vladimir Horowitz, among many other pianists.
The last and most famous of the Twelve Études, Op. 8.
Henle rates it level 8.

32/1.about: A gentle, floating piece and the first of two Poèmes that mark one of Scriabin’s first uses of the title ‘Poème’ for a short piano work — a genre label he would return to again and again for the rest of his career as his music moved away from conventional dance and character-piece titles. Marked Andante cantabile, it drifts through soft, overlapping textures without ever settling into a firm rhythmic pulse, creating the sense of something remembered or imagined rather than danced.
32/1.ctx: Composed in 1903, in the years between Scriabin’s Fourth Piano Sonata and the beginning of work on the Poem of Ecstasy, the piece sits at a turning point in his output, when he was increasingly drawn to loosely poetic, single-movement forms rather than the sonatas and character pieces of his earlier years. Its companion piece, the more turbulent Poème Op. 32 No. 2, is often paired with it in performance and recording, the two forming a contrasting pair much like the two movements of the Second Piano Sonata decades earlier.
facts: One of the first pieces Scriabin titled simply ‘Poème,’ a label he used often afterward.

49/1.ctx: Composed in 1905 as Scriabin was travelling in Switzerland, part of a set of three contrasting miniatures published together as Op. 49.

56/4.about: A terse, late miniature, the fourth of the Four Pieces, Op. 56. By this point Scriabin’s harmonic language had moved well beyond the Chopin-influenced idiom of his early études, into the dense, ambiguous chords of his mature style.
56/4.ctx: Composed in 1908, part of a set of four short, contrasting pieces (a prelude, an étude, a waltz-like piece and this étude) that show Scriabin’s harmonic language in rapid transition toward his late, mystically-charged idiom.
facts: The fourth and last of the Four Pieces, Op. 56.
Written as Scriabin’s harmonic language was moving rapidly toward his late style.

65/1.ctx: Composed in 1912, late in Scriabin’s career, the Three Études, Op. 65 are an extreme technical and harmonic experiment: each étude is built from a single interval carried through the entire piece, pushing pianism and harmony together toward the edge of tonality.
facts: No. 1 of the Three Études, Op. 65, built entirely on parallel ninths.

32/2.about: The second of the Two Poems, Op. 32, a warmer, more outgoing companion to the famous ‘Poème languide’ that opens the set. Where its companion drifts in a hazy, static harmony, this poem moves with more forward motion and a brighter close.
32/2.ctx: Composed in 1903, alongside the ‘Poème languide’, Op. 32 No. 1, one of Scriabin’s most performed miniatures. Together the pair mark an early stage of the free, one-movement ‘poem’ genre Scriabin would return to throughout the rest of his career.
facts: The second of the Two Poems, Op. 32.
Its companion, Op. 32 No. 1 (‘Poème languide’), is one of Scriabin’s best-known short pieces.

12/1.about: A flowing, Chopin-indebted impromptu, the first of two published as Op. 12, close in spirit to Scriabin’s early mazurkas and préludes and still very much within the Romantic salon tradition he inherited from Chopin and Liszt.
12/1.ctx: Composed in the mid-1890s, during the same early period as the Op. 11 préludes and Op. 8 études, when Scriabin’s style remained closely tied to Chopin’s example.
facts: The first of two Impromptus published as Op. 12.

3/10.ctx: One of the Ten Mazurkas, Op. 3, an early set of salon dances written under the direct influence of Chopin’s own mazurkas, the genre through which the young Scriabin first absorbed Chopin’s harmonic language and rubato-inflected phrasing.
facts: No. 10 of the Ten Mazurkas, Op. 3.

25/1.about: A dark, restless mazurka opening the set.
25/1.ctx: One of the Nine Mazurkas, Op. 25, a later set than the Ten Mazurkas of Op. 3, showing Scriabin’s harmonic language beginning to move beyond straightforward Chopin imitation toward the more chromatic idiom of his middle period, while keeping the mazurka’s characteristic triple-metre lilt.
facts: No. 1 of the Nine Mazurkas, Op. 25.

40/1.about: A warm, lyrical mazurka, richer in harmony than Scriabin’s earlier essays in the genre.
40/1.ctx: One of the Two Mazurkas, Op. 40, among the last works in which Scriabin returned to the Chopin-derived dance forms of his youth, by now filtered through the richer harmony of his middle period.
facts: No. 1 of the Two Mazurkas, Op. 40.
Among the last mazurkas Scriabin wrote, composed in his more harmonically advanced middle period.
